rationale: Jesus repeats the opening question about God's abandonment. Matthew quotes that question, without repeating the psalm's following clause about the speaker's transgressions.
Mark translates Jesus' cry with the psalm's opening address and question about abandonment; the remaining transgressions clause is outside the quoted words.
Both speakers describe crying to God without being heard. The psalm's day-and-night persistence and Job's complaint retain their distinct settings.
The trust and rescue of the fathers is compared with the remembered divine work for the fathers, whose deliverance is explicitly attributed to God's arm rather than their own.

The psalm remembers ancestors crying to God and being saved; Exodus recounts God hearing Israel's cry and coming to rescue them. This supplies an example, not an exclusive identification of every remembered rescue.
The psalm's speaker is a human reproach and object of contempt; Isaiah's afflicted figure is dishonored and held of no account. The worm image remains particular to the psalm.
The spectators' mocking speech and head-shaking recur among those reviling the crucified Jesus. Matthew gives the particular taunt concerning the sanctuary and self-rescue.
Mark likewise describes passersby reviling Jesus while shaking their heads, corresponding to the psalm's joined gestures and hostile speech.
The mockers' challenge that God rescue the one who trusts Him, if He desires him, closely repeats the psalm's taunt concerning trust and divine rescue.
Both prayers trace divine support to the mother's womb; this source adds being drawn from the belly and hope from the mother's breasts.
The speaker's lifelong relation to God beginning in the mother's belly corresponds to the other psalm's explicit divine support from the mother's womb.
The plea that God stay near when no helper is present is compared with Paul's report that everyone deserted his defense but the Lord stood beside him. No shared historical incident is claimed.
The enemies' open mouths are likened to a predatory lion; the other prayer asks restoration from hostile wickedness and rescue of the speaker's only life from lions.
The afflicted speaker's heart melts like wax; the other psalm uses melting wax for the removal of the wicked. The shared image is applied to different subjects.
The dried-up speaker's tongue sticks to his throat; Lamentations uses the same bodily image explicitly for nursing children suffering thirst.

The psalm says enemies dug into the speaker's hands and feet; Thomas speaks specifically of nail marks in Jesus' hands. The link compares injured hands while preserving the different wording and not supplying feet to John.
John explicitly quotes the division of garments and casting a lot for clothing, applying it to the soldiers' division and decision concerning Jesus' tunic.
Matthew narrates the division of Jesus' garments by casting a lot, matching both actions in the psalm.
Mark describes the crucifiers dividing Jesus' garments and casting a lot to determine each person's portion, corresponding to the psalm's two linked actions.
Both prayers ask God not to remain far away and to attend to the speaker's help, preserving the paired distance-and-assistance formulation.

relationship: Rescue of the soul and only one
rationale: Both pleas pair the speaker's soul with an additional expression: the only one here and the only life there. Both request rescue using hostile animal imagery, with the dog and sword here distinct from the lions there.
The psalm asks rescue from a lion's mouth; Paul reports being rescued from a lion's mouth. This verbal correspondence does not identify Paul's danger as a literal animal encounter.
Hebrews introduces the announcement of God's name to brothers and praise in the assembly as words of the One who sanctifies, directly quoting this verse.

relationship: Israel and those fearing God summoned to praise
rationale: Both calls address Israel and those who fear the Lord, summoning them to bless or praise Him. The target additionally names the houses of Aaron and Levi.
Both affirm that God regards a lowly person's prayer without treating the petition as nothing; this source also reports that the cry was heard.
Both join praise offered to God with payment of vows. The source locates this repayment before those fearing Him in the great assembly.

relationship: Seekers of God supplied with good
rationale: The needy eat and are filled while seekers praise God; the target promises that those fearing and seeking Him will lack no good thing, contrasting the hungry rich.
Both envision all nations bowing before the Lord; the source emphasizes earth's limits remembering and turning, while the target describes the nations God made coming to glorify Him.
The Lord's kingship and mastery of nations correspond to God's being King of the whole earth and reigning over nations upon His holy throne.

The psalm depicts those descending into the earth falling before God; Philippians includes those under the earth among all who bend the knee at Jesus' name. The source's eating and living soul remain distinct details.

relationship: Worship transmitted to a coming generation
rationale: The serving seed and announced coming generation correspond to a record for another generation and a people being created who will praise the Lord.
Both explicitly anticipate children or a people still to be born receiving an announcement of God's deeds, so that another generation will know and hope in Him.
The psalm presents the Lord as the speaker's shepherd; Jesus calls Himself the good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. The target develops the shepherd image through self-giving.
Isaiah directly describes the Lord shepherding, gathering and comforting His flock, corresponding to the psalm's claim that the Lord shepherds the speaker.
The green place and restful water belong to the psalm's shepherd image; Ezekiel promises God's sheep rich pasture, nourishment and rest. The geographical details remain distinct.
Both attribute personal guidance to God for His name's sake. The source speaks of righteous paths and turning the soul back; the target joins guidance with nourishment.
The speaker fears no evils while walking in death's shadow because God is with him; Isaiah promises God's presence while passing through water and fire. The dangers remain different images.

The excellent intoxicating cup corresponds to intoxication from the richness of God's house and drinking the torrent of His delight. The table, enemies and head-oil belong to this source's fuller image.
The expectation of dwelling in the Lord's house for length of days corresponds closely to the petition to dwell there all the days of one's life.
Paul quotes the Lord's ownership of the earth and its fullness in explaining food and conscience, directly reusing the psalm's declaration.
Both describe God making the earth firm upon waters; this source names seas and rivers in the foundation image.

relationship: Question about access to the holy mountain
rationale: Both ask who may enter or remain in God's holy dwelling and mountain, introducing ensuing ethical qualifications.
Both answers require integrity of heart and conduct, especially truthful treatment of neighbors and fidelity in swearing. They answer the respective questions about God's holy dwelling.

relationship: Purity of heart and divine access
rationale: Purity of heart qualifies the person who can stand in God's holy place; Jesus' blessing promises the pure in heart that they will see God. The settings of holy access and promised sight remain distinct.

relationship: Seeking the face of Jacob's God
rationale: Both describe seeking the Lord and His face. This source identifies Him as Jacob's God, while the target addresses Abraham's offspring and Jacob's sons and adds continual seeking and remembrance of wonders.
Both address gates to be opened for entry associated with the Lord. Here the King of glory enters; there a thankful righteous worshiper enters the Lord's gate.
The King of glory is powerful in war; the victory song praises the Lord who cast horse and rider into the sea and shatters wars. The target's actual description is preserved.
This repeated summons for the King of glory's entrance is compared with the petition to open the Lord's gates for a righteous worshiper. The entrants and gate descriptions are distinguished.
Both prayers explicitly state that the speaker lifted his soul to the Lord; the target places this act within a request to learn the way to walk.
Both pair personal hope or trust in God with a plea never to be put to shame. This source additionally asks that enemies not laugh.

The promise that those waiting for God will not be ashamed corresponds to Paul's scriptural assurance that everyone believing in Him will not be put to shame. This is a thematic comparison, not a claim that Paul identifies this exact verse as his quotation.
Both ask God to make known the way to walk and to teach and guide the speaker. The target adds instruction in doing God's will and guidance by His good Spirit.

relationship: Truth as a guide toward God
rationale: The source asks to be guided into divine truth; the target asks God to send light and truth and reports that they guided the speaker to His holy dwelling.
The plea to remember compassions and mercies from eternity corresponds to the declaration that the Lord's mercy is from eternity to eternity toward those who fear Him.

relationship: Sins of youth remembered or charged
rationale: The psalm asks God not to remember youthful sins; Job complains that God recorded evils and placed the sins of youth around him. The request and complaint are contrasted without equating their circumstances.
The Lord's kindness is the basis for His instruction of sinners; the other prayer likewise appeals to His goodness while asking Him to teach His ordinances.
Both connect the Lord's mercy with those keeping or seeking His covenant and testimonies or commandments. The source's truth and the target's generations remain distinct emphases.
Both appeal to the Lord's name as the ground for gracious dealing with sin. The source acknowledges its greatness; the target asks communal rescue and propitiation.
The God-fearing person receives instruction in a way; the target likewise links fear of the Lord with wisdom and understanding practiced in conduct.

The source promises land to the God-fearing person's seed; the target promises land to those waiting for the Lord and to the meek. The stated recipients are preserved rather than equated in every detail.
Both join the Lord's covenant and His name with reverence and knowledge or understanding. The source's actual stronghold wording is retained and is not replaced with a secret-friendship formula.
God's pulling the speaker's feet from a trap corresponds to the soul's rescue like a bird from a shattered hunters' trap. The bodily and bird images remain distinct.

relationship: Poverty as the basis of petition
rationale: Both speakers identify themselves as poor when asking God to attend and show mercy. The source adds aloneness; the target adds need and continual crying.
The petition to be brought out of expanding heart-afflictions corresponds to the other prayer's assurance that God will bring the soul out of distress in His righteousness.
Both prayers name unjust or causeless hatred from enemies. The target additionally asks that these enemies not rejoice over the speaker.

relationship: Hope, rescue and avoidance of shame
rationale: Both appeals combine hope in God, rescue and freedom from shame; the target explicitly invokes divine righteousness in requesting deliverance.
Both speak of God redeeming Israel: this source names all its afflictions, while the target names all its lawless deeds. The objects of redemption remain distinct.
Both speakers ask the Lord to judge them while appealing to their innocence or righteousness, making the ethical basis of the petition explicit.
The requested testing of heart and kidneys corresponds directly to the Lord's declaration that He examines hearts and tests kidneys before recompensing conduct.
The speaker asks to be tried by fire; the target recalls God trying the community by fire as silver is tested. Individual inward examination and communal testing remain distinct.

Both refuse participation in ungodly company. This source names sitting with a council of emptiness and entering with transgressors; Psalm1 distinguishes walking in ungodly counsel, standing in sinners' way and sitting with pestilent men.
The rejection of an evildoers' assembly corresponds to refusing fellowship or dwelling to arrogant and unjust speakers while favoring faithful companions.

The psalm joins washed hands among the innocent with going around the altar; Exodus prescribes hand-and-foot washing when priests approach the altar. The ritual comparison does not identify the psalm's speaker as an Aaronic priest.
Love of the house's beauty and place of glory corresponds to the beloved dwellings and longing for the Lord's courts in the target.
The plea not to perish together with men of bloodshed is compared with their being brought down to a well of corruption. The first speaker asks to be spared their fate.
Hands filled with gifts occur among lawless men of bloodshed; the target explicitly praises refusal of gifts against innocent people. The contrast concerns corrupt gifts rather than all giving.
The promise to bless the Lord in assemblies corresponds to the promise of thanksgiving and praise in a great assembly and among the people.
The Lord as the speaker's light corresponds to God lighting the speaker's lamp and darkness. Both portray divine aid through illumination.
The speaker's refusal to fear rests on God as protector; the target likewise reasons from God as refuge and strength to fearlessness amid upheaval.

The psalm maintains confidence even before an army; Elisha tells his fearful attendant not to fear the encircling force because of the greater protection with them. The narrative illustrates the stance without dating the psalm to that event.

relationship: Desire to dwell in God's house
rationale: The lifelong desire to dwell in and behold the Lord's house corresponds to longing for His courts and the blessedness of those who dwell in His house.

relationship: Rock and divine dwelling as refuge
rationale: Both combine being raised on a rock with protection in God's dwelling. The images express security in trouble rather than identifying a single literal site.
The personal resolve to seek God's face corresponds directly to the summons to seek His face continually.

relationship: Plea against the hidden divine face
rationale: Both ask that God not turn His face away from the distressed speaker; the target states the feared consequence as becoming like those descending to a pit.
The Lord receives the one abandoned by father and mother; Isaiah contrasts even a mother's possible forgetting with God's refusal to forget Zion. The human relationships remain distinct.
Both request instruction or guidance along God's upright way specifically because of enemies, preserving the same motive and path image.

The psalm's unjust witnesses are compared with false witnesses sought and appearing against Jesus before the council. This is a correspondence of hostile testimony, not a claim that the psalm narrates that hearing.

relationship: Hope in the land of the living
rationale: Expectation of seeing the Lord's good things in the land of the living corresponds to calling Him one's hope and portion in that land.
Both exhort those waiting or hoping for the Lord to act courageously and let their hearts be strong, sharing the distinctive paired commands.

relationship: Divine withdrawal and descent to the pit
rationale: Both fear becoming like those descending to a pit if God withholds attention. Silence toward the petitioner and turning the face away are the respective descriptions.

The psalm depicts hands lifted toward the holy temple; Solomon spreads his hands before the altar in the temple court and toward heaven. The posture and sanctuary context correspond while the directions remain explicit.
Both describe people speaking peaceful things while inwardly devising evil or deceit, exposing the discrepancy between speech and intention.

The plea that evildoers receive according to their works corresponds to the declaration that God repays each according to works. The enemy-directed petition and universal judgment statement remain distinct.
The requested repayment according to practices corresponds to the Lord's declaration that He gives each according to ways and the fruits of practices.

relationship: Disregard of God's works and judgment
rationale: Both connect failure to consider the Lord's works or the works of His hands with judgment. The source describes being pulled down; Isaiah describes captivity and death.
Both bless God immediately in connection with His hearing the sound of a petition and not rejecting prayer.
Both explicitly attribute the anointed one's salvation to the Lord; the target describes the saving strength of His right hand.
The plea to save and shepherd God's people corresponds to the invocation of Israel's shepherd and the call for Him to come and save.

relationship: Glory and honor brought to the Lord
rationale: Both repeat the summons to bring glory and honor to the Lord. This source addresses sons of God and mentions young rams; the target addresses families of nations.

relationship: Glory for the name and worship in the holy court
rationale: The invitation to give glory for the Lord's name and bow in His holy courtyard closely recurs in the target's adjoining calls.
The Lord's voice over many waters and the God of glory's thunder correspond to waters fearing God and His thundering voice amid lightning and trembling earth.

The description of divine thunder corresponds to the Lord thundering with a great voice against Israel's attackers. The narrative supplies an example of the voice's power, not the identity of the psalm's waters.
The Lord's strong and magnificent voice is compared with Elihu's description of the Strong One thundering wonders with His voice. The attribution to Elihu is retained.
The Lord crushing Lebanon's cedars corresponds to the Lord's day against the high cedars of Lebanon among the proud and elevated. No particular storm or campaign is identified.

The Lord's voice shakes the wilderness of Kadesh; Hebrews describes His voice shaking the earth and promising a further shaking. The geographic scope differs, and this is not labeled Hebrews' quoted source.
The Lord's sitting as King for ever corresponds to His remaining for ever with a throne prepared for judgment. The flood statement is an additional feature of this source.
The psalm's promise that the Lord bless His people with peace corresponds to the priestly blessing culminating in the Lord giving peace.
The speaker thanks God for not gladdening his enemies; the other prayer asks that unjust enemies not rejoice over him. The answered thanksgiving and request correspond.
The report of crying to God and being healed is compared with the direct plea for the Lord to heal the weak speaker. No shared illness or chronology is assumed.
Being brought up from Hades corresponds to confidence that God will not abandon the speaker's soul to Hades. The images of deliverance retain their own temporal forms.
Both summon God's people to rejoice or sing and give thanks at the remembrance of His holiness, sharing this specific thanksgiving formula.

Evening weeping followed by morning exultation is compared with sowing in tears and returning with exultation. The comparison concerns the reversal and does not rewrite the source's wrath clause as a statement of duration.
The speaker recalls saying in prosperity that he would never be shaken; the sinner in Psalm9 says he will not be shaken across generations. Their similar boasts have different speakers and contexts.

relationship: Trouble when God turns His face away
rationale: Both explicitly connect God turning His face away with the recipients becoming troubled. Here the individual speaks; the target describes dependent creatures.

relationship: Question about thanksgiving among the dead
rationale: Both appeal for life by asking whether death or Hades permits thanksgiving to God. The source uses dust and corruption as its images.

relationship: Life as the setting of praise
rationale: The question whether dust can thank God corresponds to the contrast between the dead who do not praise Him and the living who bless Him.
The Lord hearing and becoming the speaker's helper corresponds to thanksgiving that He heard and became the speaker's salvation.
The torn sackcloth and girding with gladness correspond to mourners receiving an ointment of joy and a robe of glory instead of despondency. The texts use distinct clothing images for the reversal.
Both combine hope in God, avoidance of disgrace and rescue in divine righteousness, with closely corresponding requests to be brought out.
Both ask God to bend His ear, save the speaker and become a defending or protecting place of refuge.
Both attribute the speaker's guidance to the Lord for His name's sake; nourishment here accompanies the target's righteous paths and restored soul.
The promise of release from a hidden trap corresponds to the rescued soul likened to a bird escaping when hunters' trap is shattered.

relationship: Words used by Jesus at death
rationale: Jesus entrusts His spirit into the Father's hands using the psalm's distinctive formula. Luke gives this as His final spoken prayer before death.
Stephen asks the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit while being stoned, corresponding to the psalm's act of entrusting the spirit to the Lord. The addressee and wording are preserved.
Both negatively describe those guarding vain things; the psalm contrasts them with hope in the Lord, while Jonah says such people abandoned their mercy.

The report that God looked upon humiliation and saved from constraints is compared with His seeing Israel's affliction and coming to rescue them from Egypt. This is an illustrative correspondence without assigning the psalm to that event.

relationship: From enemies into a spacious place
rationale: Both describe divine rescue from enemies through the image of being brought or set in a spacious place.
Both use the specific description of the speaker's eye being troubled from anger. This source additionally names soul and belly.
Both describe bodily weakness, troubled bones and prolonged groaning. The source expressly locates weakness in poverty, without replacing that word with sin.

The speaker becomes a reproach to neighbors and a fear to acquaintances, while outside observers flee; the target distinguishes friends and neighbors standing opposite from the nearest standing far away. The comparison preserves these different reactions within nearby relationships.

relationship: Living speaker likened to forgotten dead
rationale: The speaker describes being forgotten like a dead person; the target similarly likens the speaker to helpless dead in a grave who are remembered no more.
Both speakers report hearing the reproach of many gathering all around and plotting against them. The close verbal correspondence preserves their different settings.
The declaration that the speaker's seasons are in God's hands corresponds to human months being numbered with God and a limit set by Him.

relationship: The shining divine face and mercy
rationale: The plea that God's face shine upon His servant and save in mercy corresponds to the blessing that His face shine and He show mercy.
Both prayers oppose deceitful lips and arrogant speech: one asks that they become speechless, the other that the Lord destroy them. The source specifically names their attacks on the righteous.
Both depict divine protection with dwelling imagery: the source promises shelter in a tent from human strife, while the target joins sojourning in God's dwelling with shelter beneath His wings.

relationship: Cast from God's eyes yet heard
rationale: Both prayers report the speaker's claim of being cast from God's eyes alongside divine hearing of the cry. The psalm's alarm and Jonah's descent into the sea remain separate settings.

relationship: Paired exhortation to courage and strength
rationale: The exhortation to those hoping in the Lord to be courageous and strong corresponds to the paired commands to be courageous and strong while standing firm in faith.
Paul introduces David's declaration of blessedness and directly quotes forgiveness of lawless deeds and covering of sins.
Paul directly quotes the blessedness of the man whose sin the Lord does not reckon. The psalm's additional no-deceit clause is outside that quotation.

relationship: Same-chapter movement from silence to confession
rationale: Silence accompanies bodily decline and crying; the later acknowledgment of sin accompanies reported forgiveness. The source's simultaneous silence and crying are preserved, while the comparison follows the psalm's change to open confession.
The psalm describes God's hand weighing heavily day and night; Job asks that the divine hand and terror be removed. The source's thorn and misery are not supplied to Job.
The speaker acknowledges rather than covers lawlessness and reports forgiveness; the letter likewise connects confession of sins with God's forgiving and cleansing.
The praying person's safety from a flood is compared with God as refuge even when seas roar and mountains are displaced into them. The particular water images remain distinct.
The promise of instruction in the way corresponds to the other prayer's request that God teach His paths and guide in truth. The speaker of this promise is not assigned an identity beyond the verse.

relationship: A horse controlled through its mouth
rationale: Both employ the horse's bridle or bit as an image of guidance and restraint. The psalm warns against uncomprehending behavior; James uses the animal illustration in discussing control of speech.

This source assigns many scourges to the sinner and mercy to the hopeful; the target assigns many afflictions to the righteous yet promises rescue. The comparison preserves the different subjects rather than treating suffering as proof of guilt.
Both summon the righteous and upright to exult in the Lord, linking upright character with the appropriateness of praise.
The exhortation to righteous and upright people to exult in the Lord closely corresponds to the previous psalm's concluding summons to those groups.
Both join thanksgiving and music to the Lord with the lyre and a ten-stringed psaltery, preserving the specified instruments.

relationship: A new song to the Lord
rationale: Both command singing a new song to the Lord; this source adds skilled music and a triumphal shout, while the target addresses all the earth.
The Lord's upright word and faithful works correspond to the proclamation that God's works are true and He is faithful, righteous and without unrighteousness.

relationship: The earth full of divine mercy
rationale: Both explicitly declare the earth full of the Lord's mercy. The target turns this declaration into a request for instruction.

The psalm attributes the heavens to the Lord's word; Genesis narrates God speaking the firmament into being and naming it Heaven. The spirit of His mouth and all their power remain this source's additional expressions.
God's gathering the waters in the psalm corresponds to His command that waters gather and the resulting seas in Genesis. The wineskin and storehouses belong to the psalm's imagery.
The collected waters and stored deeps correspond to the Lord's account of bounding the sea with gates and bars. The containment images are compared without making them identical structures.

relationship: The whole earth trembling before God
rationale: Both call the entire earth and its inhabitants to be shaken before the Lord; the target places this call alongside worship in His holy court.
The declaration that God spoke and things came to be is illustrated directly by His command for light and the appearance of light.
The nullification of nations', peoples' and rulers' counsels is compared with their concerted opposition meeting divine laughter and wrath in Psalm2.
Both contrast human plans with the Lord's counsel remaining for ever, using the same enduring-counsel formulation.
The chosen people called the Lord's inheritance correspond to Jacob and Israel explicitly designated His portion and measured lot of inheritance.
Both describe the Lord looking down from heaven upon the sons of men, preserving the vantage point and the people observed.
The Lord surveys the earth's inhabitants from His dwelling; the target joins His heavenly throne and holy temple with eyes toward the needy and eyelids examining the sons of men.
The maker of individual hearts understands deeds; the other prayer joins God's understanding of personal reasonings and ways with His forming the speaker.
The denial that great force or a giant's strength saves corresponds to David's declaration that the Lord does not save by sword and spear because the battle belongs to Him.

relationship: A war horse cannot supply salvation
rationale: The horse's power is denied as a source of salvation; the proverb likewise distinguishes a horse prepared for war from the help that comes from the Lord.

relationship: Horses contrasted with reliance on God
rationale: The horse's inability to save corresponds to the contrast between reliance on chariots and horses and reliance on the Lord's name, followed by their different outcomes.

relationship: The Lord's eyes upon His faithful
rationale: Both explicitly place the Lord's eyes upon those devoted to Him: those fearing and hoping here, and the righteous there.
The Lord nourishes the hopeful in famine; the target likewise promises that the blameless will be filled during famine rather than shamed in adversity.

relationship: Hope in the divine helper and defender
rationale: The waiting soul calls the Lord helper and defender; the target repeatedly joins Israel's, Aaron's and God-fearers' hope with those same two descriptions.

relationship: Rejoicing joined to hope in the divine name
rationale: The community's rejoicing in God and hope in His holy name correspond to Psalm5's call for those hoping in Him to rejoice and those loving His name to boast in Him. The combined name, hope and rejoicing language supplies the specific reciprocal comparison.
